The Court must deny Jon Davidson’s motion to compel arbitration because arbitration is strictly a matter of consent, not coercion. Davidson is a nonsignatory to the original agreement between Harper Investors and Gold Reserve & Lending. As established in *Lorber Industries of California v. Los Angeles Printworks Corp.*, the right to enforce an arbitration provision is fundamentally contractual and generally limited to the signatories, their agents, or intended beneficiaries. Davidson fits none of these categories.

First, there is no contractual privity. At the time Harper Investors signed their agreements, Davidson was not a party to the transaction. The investors never agreed to arbitrate disputes with him personally. Under established contract principles, the parties did not intend to confer enforcement rights upon an unknown future owner. Therefore, Davidson cannot claim third-party beneficiary status to retrofit the contract for his defense.

Second, the dispute does not "arise out of or relate to" the original contract. Davidson’s alleged liability stems from independent fraudulent acts committed through separate entities, such as the Fund Restoration Alliance and Tax Support Circle. These allegations involve soliciting funds and discouraging lawsuits long after the original contract was executed. Mere subsequent ownership of Gold Reserve does not grant Davidson standing to use the company’s prior contracts as a shield against personal liability for separate, later-occurring torts.

To permit Davidson to compel arbitration would force Harper Investors into a forum they never agreed to, regarding disputes wholly separate from the original investment contract. Because Davidson lacks the requisite standing as a nonsignatory and the claims fall outside the contract’s scope, Harper Investors must prevail.
